newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries take GDP report in stride--experts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries take GDP report in stride--experts.

text.p: U.S. credit market players dumped government securities on news of explosive economic growth in the first quarter, but later the data proved less worrisome as experts bet the economy would soon throttle down.
After sinking as much as 20/32, the benchmark Treasury bond was trading about 1/2 point higher as players' focus shifted away from the report on Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
"That was discarded for two reasons: one, it was ancient history and the surprise was in inventories," said Carey Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.
"And because the surprise was in a stronger inventory guessed by the Commerce Department, people thought it might borrow from second quarter growth," he added.

GDP expanded in the first three months at a 5.6 percent annual pace, its largest gain since a 6.0 percent rise in the fourth quarter of 1987. Consumers spent heavily, and businesses added a staggering $46.1 billion to inventories.

Bond yields rose to 7.037 percent shortly after the data, but Treasuries wiped out their modest losses by midday amid rising hopes that the White House and Congress would soon strike a deal for a balanced budget.
GDP was only one in a batch of potentially market moving economic indicators due out this week.
A Labor Department report on Tuesday showed the employment cost index (ECI) rose 0.6 percent in the first quarter, a rise below the 0.9 percent gain expected in a Reuters poll.

On Thursday, Treasury market participants will scrutinize the National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) manufacturing activity report for April. Friday will bring the release of crucial U.S. employment data for the same month.
Of these major economic figures, experts ranked GDP as less important.

A bill trader at a major bank deemed gains in Treasuries on Wednesday as a "continuation of a short-covering rally, thinking that GDP (is) not as a big deal as maybe NAPM or payrolls would be towards the end of this week."

Should the NAPM index and the payrolls report prove benign, the market will be less concerned about the potential for another Federal Reserve rate rise and Treasuries will continue to trade well, the trader said.
After the GDP figures hit the market, some economists had warned the Fed may decide to tighten credit again.
By contrast, newspapers had just reported less concern the Fed would raise rates following the release of the ECI.
Some traders expressed frustration with the rapidly shifting views on central bank policy.
"Yesterday you got good news. Today you got bad news. Who knows what we're going to get tomorrow?" said a trader at a major Wall Street investment house.
